blocks.content: Choose a descending speed that leaves room to brake, steer, and stop within what you can see. This lesson practices position and early decisions; it does not use timed runs or an aero tuck to chase speed.

blocks.title: A descent changes under the wheels
blocks.content: A rider crests a familiar gravel descent and sees loose stones below a bend. The useful work begins at the crest: scan the visible road, choose a comfortable speed, and keep the hands ready to brake. There is no time bonus worth entering the loose section faster than you can steer or stop.

blocks.label: Stable feet, usable brakes
blocks.content: On a gentle descent, keep your feet supported on the pedals, arms bent enough to absorb bumps, and both hands securely on the bars near the brake levers. Let the bike move beneath you without hanging your weight on the bars. If your position makes it harder to see, steer, or reach a brake, reset to a more upright, familiar stance.

### Read the descent before you commit

At the crest, look as far as the visible road allows. Find bends, surface changes, riders, traffic, and places where you could stop. Begin slowing before a blind section or a loose patch. Use both brakes gradually while the bike is mostly upright, then ease heavy pressure as you steer. Keep enough room to choose a different line if the gravel moves.

The drops can give some riders a secure grip and good brake access. Practice that hand position on easy ground first. If the hoods give you better control on your bike, stay there. No hand position makes a blind corner safe at speed.

items.title: Body position changes with the road
items.content:
A steeper descent can shift more load toward the front wheel, especially under braking. Keep the feet supporting you and your arms available to absorb bumps. You may move your hips to stay balanced, but there is no gradient chart that tells every rider how far back to go. Moving too far behind the saddle can also make the front wheel harder to guide.

Choose a position that keeps both wheels tracking, lets you see ahead, and leaves full access to the brakes. Ask a coach to check your position if you cannot find that balance on a gentle slope.

blocks.title: The Position Ladder
blocks.description: Move only as far into a lower stance as control and visibility allow. Climb back to the stable stance whenever conditions change.

steps.detail: Feet supported, arms bent, eyes on the visible road, hands ready to brake.

steps.action: Choose the hand position you have practiced
steps.detail: Use hoods or drops only where you can steer and reach both levers securely.
Move the hips only enough to keep the bike tracking under you. Avoid hanging off the bars or far behind the saddle.
Sit or stand more upright when you need a better view, more brake access, or room to react.
Use both brakes smoothly on the approach; keep room for a wider line when the surface changes.

blocks.title: Position and Visibility Check
blocks.description: Use a gentle, familiar descent with a clear runout and no traffic. Repeat at a comfortable speed to compare control and brake access, not elapsed time.

variants.label: One easy descent
steps: Check the descent on foot or at an easy pace. Leave if the surface, sightline, or traffic makes it unsuitable.
Ride down once in the hand position you normally use. Notice where you can see and when you begin slowing.
If you have practiced riding in the drops, repeat at the same easy pace and compare grip and brake access.
Keep the position that gives you more control. Stop the session if either position makes steering or braking uncertain.

variants.label: One visible surface change
steps: On a familiar easy descent, identify a visible change in surface before you roll in.
Choose a comfortable speed before that change, keeping both hands ready to brake.
After stopping safely, write down what you saw and whether your position left room to react. Do not time the run.

proof_gate.description: You can descend an easy, visible slope with secure hands, clear sightline, and unhurried braking.
proof_gate.target: Repeatable control with no elapsed-time or maximum-speed target

blocks.caption: What to do when a descent changes
rows: A bend or surface change is visible ahead
Look through it, slow on the approach, and keep a clear runout
Reduce speed until you can stop within what you can see
Your hand position limits brake access
Return to a position where you can use both brakes securely
A tire starts to push or skid
Avoid abrupt inputs, make room, and stop the drill when safe

blocks.title: How to Descend on a Gravel Bike
blocks.caption: Gravel descending technique — body position and line choice at speed.

blocks.title: Gravel Gods // Ep. 5 // Let The Pros Handle It
blocks.caption: Long-form: watch pros ride technical gravel at speed. Notice how relaxed and low they stay, how early they brake, and how they let the bike move. This is descending as play, done well.

blocks.question: A familiar gravel descent steepens before a bend, and the surface turns loose. What is the useful sequence?

options.text: Look ahead, slow smoothly before the loose bend, and use a secure position with both brakes accessible
Tuck to gain speed, then brake hard while leaned into the bend
Move as far behind the saddle as possible because the grade is steep
Keep the same speed because the descent is familiar

blocks.explanation: The known road has changed. Set a comfortable speed while you can see and steer, and use a position that keeps both brakes available. No fixed hip offset or aero target replaces that decision.

blocks.content: On your next easy descent, note where you first saw the bend, where you began slowing, and which hand position gave you the best control. Keep the run untimed.
Next lesson: Pack Dynamics & Pacing by Terrain. You will use the same sightline and control checks when another rider is ahead of you.
